_comment: Study paths rendered by paths.html. Each step's html is trusted site-authored content (never API or user text). Paths order existing, sourced material only — they must not introduce new claims; every linked page carries its own verification badges. Adding a path = adding an entry here. Structured fields alongside html: page is the clean path of the tool page the step uses (null when the step happens on the previous page), label is the short step name shown in the path ribbon, minutes is a rough time estimate; path.minutes must equal the sum of its steps' (check-paths.mjs enforces all of this).

paths.title: Follow a root through the Qur'an
paths.intro: Take r-ḥ-m (mercy) from a single verse to its full corpus distribution.

steps.label: Read the root in context
steps.html: Read it in context: al-Fatihah 1:1 — two of the four words carry the root.

steps.label: Open the root's profile
steps.html: Open the root's profile: r-ḥ-m on Roots — 339 occurrences, derived forms, Makki/Madani split, every verse reference.

steps.label: Scan its co-occurring roots
steps.html: See what it travels with: the co-occurring roots section on the same page — gh-f-r (forgiveness) is its most frequent verse-level companion.

steps.label: Compare two passages
steps.html: Compare passages where it clusters: al-Fatihah vs the opening of Maryam in Compare's Passages mode.

paths.title: Profile a surah before reading it
paths.intro: Build a structural picture of a surah from the data, then read it with that frame.

steps.label: Open a surah's profile
steps.html: On Navigate, open the Profile panel for a surah (try 103, al-'Asr): verse count, distinct roots, top roots, chronological period.

steps.label: Check the era pattern
steps.html: Check its length band against the era pattern on Numbers (verse length by period).

steps.label: Read at Study depth
steps.html: Read it end to end on Read at Study depth (press 2) with word-by-word morphology on.

steps.label: Take the outline exercise
steps.html: Test your structural reading in the al-'Asr outline exercise.

paths.title: Trace a claim to its source
paths.intro: The site's core discipline: never take a number on trust — including ours.

steps.label: Pick a claim
steps.html: Pick a claim on Numbers, for example the top-five root frequencies.

steps.label: Open its citation badge
steps.html: Click its badge (●): the popover shows the full Chicago-style citation of the source.

steps.label: Follow the source
steps.html: Follow the source entry on Sources to the primary corpus at corpus.quran.com and check one number yourself.

steps.label: Run a triangulation prompt
steps.html: Run a triangulation prompt from Validation against an independent tool, and see whether it converges on the same figure.

paths.title: Study a theme end to end
paths.intro: Move from a life theme to the passages where its vocabulary clusters, and form your own reading of what they agree on.

steps.label: Pick a theme gateway
steps.html: Pick a gateway on Themes (try Forgiveness) and note its root families — the gateway is lexical, a starting point rather than an index.

steps.label: Read its key passages
steps.html: Open two or three of its key passages on the Read page and read each whole discourse around the verse, not just the verse itself.

steps.label: Compare the top passages
steps.html: Use the theme card's "top two passages side by side" link to see, in Compare, which roots the passages actually share.

steps.label: Follow the top root
steps.html: Follow the theme's most frequent root into Roots: where else does it cluster, and in which period? Write down what the passages agree on and where they differ.

paths.title: Test a Khan outline against the site's own computed signals
paths.intro: Propose your own structure, reveal Dr. Khan's published outline, then see what the site's mechanical tools find — or don't find — in the same surah.

steps.label: Propose your own outline
steps.html: Work through the al-'Alaq outline exercise: propose your own verse-by-verse structure before revealing Khan's.

steps.label: Read the computed signals
steps.html: Open the same surah's Dossier. Its Structure section shows the site's own computed discursive pivots, rhetorical features, and mechanically segmented sections for this exact surah, plus its Rhyme and Formulas sections. Al-'Alaq is one of the few Khan-outline surahs where the computed segmentation finds more than one section (3, from a 19-verse surah), so the block-mirror tests actually have something to test here, though none of them reached significance. The ring-composition proxy is a corpus-wide test with no surviving result in any surah, so the Dossier reports it as no result rather than showing one; read both tests on Patterns. Not every mechanical detector finds something significant, and a non-significant result is itself a datum, not a gap.

steps.label: Follow a signal to its method
steps.html: Follow whichever signal caught your eye to its full method and corpus-wide result on Patterns.

steps.label: Write up the comparison
steps.html: Return to Read at Study depth and write in the discovery worksheet where Khan's outline and the site's computed signals agree, diverge, or simply don't overlap.
